# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

AI Policy Landscape Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) (House discussion draft) · 2026
 Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA)
 GAAIA A House discussion draft released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, organized into four titles: frontier AI governance, workforce, cybersecurity, and research and international cooperation. It federalizes the SB 53 / RAISE-style transparency model — large frontier developers (>$500M revenue) must write and publicly post a frontier AI framework, file pre-deployment reports, and report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days (or 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury), backed by fines of up to $1M per day and federal and state AG injunctions. CAISI is established in statute within the Department of Commerce to set voluntary security standards and to license Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) that audit developer frameworks. Its preemption clause is deliberately narrow: it bars only state laws specifically targeting AI model development, expressly preserves laws of general applicability, common law remedies, and regulation of AI use and deployment, and sunsets three years after enactment. Title II builds the most elaborate AI workforce-data apparatus of any proposal — WARN Act layoff disclosures, AI-sensitive occupation forecasts, an AI Workforce Research Hub, and a study of a Rapid AI Adjustment Assistance Program.
 Key Provisions
 CAISI established in statute within Commerce, setting voluntary AI security standards and licensing Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) to audit frontier developers
 Large frontier developers (>$500M revenue) must publish a frontier AI framework, file pre-deployment reports, and report critical safety incidents (15 days, or 24 hours if imminent), with fines up to $1M/day
 Narrow, three-year-sunsetting preemption of state laws targeting AI model development only — preserving common law and regulation of AI use and deployment
 WARN Act amended to require disclosure when AI is a 'substantial factor' in a qualifying mass layoff, including the share of job losses attributable to AI
 AI Workforce Research Hub, prediction-interval forecasts for AI-sensitive occupations, and a study of a Rapid AI Adjustment Assistance Program modeled on trade adjustment assistance
 Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, increased AI fraud penalties, statutory NAIRR, and international standards coalitions that exclude China absent WTO certification
 Regulatory Philosophy
 Structured but light-touch federalism that codifies the emerging transparency consensus rather than imposing pre-deployment gates. Obernolte's draft accepts a real federal disclosure-and-audit regime for the largest frontier developers while keeping CAISI's technical standards voluntary, and pairs it with an unusually deep investment in measuring AI's labor-market impact. Its preemption is narrow and time-limited — confined to model development and sunsetting in three years — a marked departure from the broad, permanent preemption sought by the White House and the Blackburn bill.
 Where the burden falls
 Frontier Primary Apps Secondary Hyperscalers None Chips None Base assessed Frontier developers above $500M; employers conducting AI-driven layoffs Why it lands there The frontier-governance title uses the same $500M selector as the state laws it federalizes, so its transparency and audit obligations land on the frontier layer. Title II is the interesting part: amending the WARN Act to require disclosure when AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff assesses the employer doing the deploying, not the developer selling the model, which reaches the app layer and enterprise adopters. Two titles, two different layers. Compare all proposals by layer → In contrast
 GAAIA vs. the OpenAI Blueprint
 GAAIA and OpenAI's Blueprint share an architecture — a statutory CAISI, the SB 53 / RAISE transparency model, and third-party verification (GAAIA's licensed IVOs mirror the Blueprint's certified assessors). They diverge on teeth and scope. GAAIA pairs a soft trigger (disclosure, with no government evaluation gate) with hard enforcement — $1M/day fines and federal and state AG injunctions — and ranges across workforce data, fraud, and education. The Blueprint inverts this: a mandatory CAISI pre-release evaluation (a harder trigger) that is purely advisory, since CAISI can recommend but never block, paired with a single-minded focus on catastrophic CBRN, cyber, and recursive-self-improvement risk that brackets workers entirely. And where GAAIA is operative legislative text, the Blueprint is industry advocacy.
 Compare with OpenAI Blueprint → Strengths
 Derived from the proposal’s own policy documents
 + Federalizes the SB 53 / RAISE transparency model with real teeth — $1M/day fines, federal and state AG injunctions, and licensed third-party IVO audits of developer frameworks 
 + Preemption is narrow and self-sunsetting (three years, model development only), preserving common law remedies and states' authority over AI use and deployment — a far lighter touch than the White House or Blackburn 
 + Title II is the most serious workforce effort in the landscape: WARN Act AI-layoff disclosures, AI-sensitive occupation forecasts, and a research hub that would finally generate systematic evidence on displacement 
 + Strong whistleblower protections — reinstatement, double back pay with interest, and attorney's fees — give insiders a safe channel to report frontier-AI violations 
 + Pragmatic, bipartisan-flavored construction that codifies CAISI and NAIRR and funds open-source security and testbeds, giving it a more plausible path to passage than messaging-oriented bills 
 Weaknesses
 From the perspective of political opposition
 − Transparency and framework audits are not pre-deployment gates — like SB 53 and RAISE, it lets companies ship frontier models first and disclose risks after, with no authority to stop a dangerous release 
 − CAISI's core standards remain voluntary, and the binding obligations reach only a handful of >$500M developers, leaving the vast majority of AI systems untouched 
 − The workforce title is overwhelmingly studies, forecasts, reports, and pilots — it measures displacement meticulously but creates no benefits, no redistribution, and only a study of an adjustment program rather than the program itself 
 − It is silent on the harms states have actually legislated against — child safety, algorithmic discrimination, deepfakes, and copyright — even while preempting a slice of state authority over development 
 − IVO immunity from loss claims, combined with broad trade-secret and security redactions, could hollow out accountability by letting developers and their paid auditors control what the public and regulators ever see 
 − The preemption line itself is contestable: it bars only state laws 'specifically targeting' model development while preserving deployment

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. {"content": "# Staff Q&A: GAAIA discussion draft

Prepared for ACIA staff ahead of Energy and Commerce meetings. Answers capped at 120 words.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

They answer different questions. Preemption is about jurisdiction: one national standard instead of fifty conflicting ones, and 61% of our members say conflicting state definitions are their top compliance problem. Incident reporting is a substantive mandate, and lighter is not the same as justified. Section 111 defines reportable events to include "loss of control" of a model and "failure of risk-mitigation measures," categories with no documented cases behind them, and it attaches penalties reported at up to $1 million per day. Federalizing a mandate does not fix its premise; it nationalizes it. Incidents that are real, such as stolen model weights, are already cyber intrusions reportable to CISA and the FBI under existing law. Strike the provision.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Obligations tied to harms we can point to. We accept federal enforcement of existing law against fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects, and GAAIA's Section 121 preserves state common law remedies and state authority over AI use and deployment, which is where actual consumer harms show up. We support voluntary, industry-led standards, which is how NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and the ANSI and ISO channels already work. We support Title III's open-source security grants and the testbeds in Title IV. What we cannot accept are mandates premised on "catastrophic risk" thresholds, pre-deployment gates, incident reporting to a new federal AI safety bureau, or a licensed auditor regime. # Comment letter: ACIA to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, DC

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a discussion draft and for inviting stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington coalition of about 140 artificial intelligence developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture investors. Our members train the models, fabricate the chips and run the facilities behind American AI. Many are already living under the California and New York frontier laws that this draft would interact with, so our comments come from experience rather than theory.

Our position is straightforward. We support the preemption in Section 121 and most of Titles III and IV. We oppose the CAISI codification in Section 102 and the mandates in Sections 111 and 112, because they write an unfounded narrative about catastrophic AI risk into federal law. We ask you to strike those provisions, make preemption permanent, and keep the parts of the draft that actually help American builders.

## 1. The draft legislates a premise the evidence does not support

Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or of more than $1 billion in property damage. It defines "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of frontier model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. Section 101 also defines "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," language that reappears throughout Section 112.

Those definitions are the load-bearing wall of Title I. And they describe risks for which there is no evidence. No current or reasonably foreseeable AI system has caused a mass-casualty event or escaped human control. The scenarios that animate these provisions come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations. "Dangerous capability" evaluations and "scheming" studies are staged setups: they measure how a model behaves when researchers construct elaborate prompts inside fictional environments, which tells you little or nothing about how a deployed system behaves in the real world.

Congress should also ask who supplies these scenarios. The advocacy network behind them is small and unusually well funded. Open Philanthropy, renamed Coefficient Giving in late 2025, reported that its technical AI safety grantmaking rose from $46 million in 2024 to $157 million in 2025, across more than 200 grants. That money sustains a professional apparatus of grantees, coalitions and campaigns with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. Sections 102, 111 and 112 would convert that movement's premises into federal law, with a federal office, a licensed audit industry and a $100 million annual line item to enforce them.

Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years. That is a telling admission: their authors expect the underlying evidence question to still be open in 2029. A mandate that cannot survive a reauthorization fight should not be enacted in the first place.

## 2. Our members are already paying for this narrative

ACIA surveyed its members in August 2026, and we are happy to share the aggregate results with your staff.

Among surveyed developers above $500 million in revenue that maintain a published frontier safety framework, the median estimated cost of keeping that framework current is $1.4 million per year. Across all surveyed developers, the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function is $310,000. Developers complying with the California and New York regimes in parallel report a median of 6.5 full-time employees devoted to that work. Thirty-four percent of surveyed startups say they delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and 61 percent of members cite conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.

Those figures are the case for Section 121 and against Sections 111 and 112. A federal reporting mandate does not relieve the burden of state mandates. It adds a third layer on top of them, with federal penalties attached.

## 3. Preemption: support it, and make it permanent

We strongly support Section 121, which preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models while expressly preserving laws of general applicability, common law remedies, and state authority over AI use and deployment. California's SB 53 (Chapter 138 of 2025) has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour reporting clock. Developers cannot build against a map that redraws itself, and investors will not underwrite projects that face a new compliance cliff every few years.

Two changes would make Section 121 work as intended.

First, remove the three-year sunset. A preemption that expires in 2029 tells state legislatures to keep drafting, because their bills simply queue up for the day the freeze lifts. It also tells our members to keep paying for parallel state compliance, since the relief is temporary. The December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI and the White House's March 20, 2026 legislative framework both argue that state laws imposing undue burdens should give way to a minimally burdensome national standard. GAAIA should deliver that, not a three-year truce.

Second, tighten the development and deployment line. An ac
... [564 chars truncated] ...
ent within 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Combined with the civil penalty exposure elsewhere in the draft, reported at up to $1 million per day, this creates enormous liability attached to definitional disputes.

We ask you to strike it, for three reasons.

The definitions sweep in non-events. "Loss of control" and "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" are categories built for hypothetical scenarios, not documented ones. A company could be reporting, and paying penalties over, incidents that harmed no one.

Real incidents already have reporting channels. Unauthorized access to model weights is a computer intrusion, already a federal crime, and companies already report such intrusions to CISA and the FBI. A federal AI-specific mechanism adds a second, parallel obligation without adding a single responder.

And the mandate itself creates risk. A federal registry of AI security weaknesses, held by a new office with a small staff, is a target. Congress should not require companies to centralize sensitive security information with an agency that has no operational mission to use it.

## 5. CAISI: strike Section 102, and do not fund it

Section 102 codifies CAISI inside the Department of Commerce, hands it a portfolio of voluntary standards, system evaluation, monitoring of AI progress, synthetic content detection and the entire IVO licensing regime, and authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority charged to IVOs and large frontier developers. Your own FAQ notes that is an order of magnitude above the center's current roughly $15 million budget.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we are asking appropriators not to fund the center at all. The administration created CAISI administratively in June 2025 out of the U.S. AI Safety Institute. There is no statutory gap to fill, and there is no evidence of harm that justifies a tenfold budget increase plus a permanent statutory home.

The White House's March 20, 2026 framework told Congress not to create any new federal rulemaking body to regulate AI. A licensed auditor regime supervised by a statutory CAISI is that body by another name. Section 112 would let the CAISI Director license independent verification organizations, send them into developers twice a year and on demand, and have them refer findings to the attorney general and state attorneys general. The auditors would depend on the office for their licenses and on the audited companies for their fees. That is textbook regulatory capture, and it would land on a handful of American developers while their foreign competitors face nothing comparable.

None of this means we oppose standards. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework worked precisely because it was voluntary, industry-led and usable. The International Organization for Standardization and the American National Standards Institute channels work, and the Title IV standards coordination that expressly excludes China is the right instinct. Keep that work voluntary and keep it at NIST's measurement science mission, not in a new federal AI safety bureau.

## 6. What we support and ask you to keep

We support Section 301, which extends the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035 so companies can share threat information without antitrust exposure. We support Section 311, authorizing CISA to grant funds to maintainers of widely used critical open-source software, though we would remove the CAISI consultation role. We support Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security. We support the Title IV testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and the National Science Foundation, the codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, and the international standards work that expressly excludes China absent World Trade Organization certification. We support Section 122's Government Accountability Office review of federal AI adoption and of statutes that burden AI infrastructure, and Section 141's examination of agency pressure on AI platforms.

On Title II, we support better labor market data, including the Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics survey changes, and we would ask that it stay measurement rather than become a platform for new mandates. On Section 113, we support whistleblower protection and ask that "AI violations" be limited to violations of this Act rather than any violation of any federal law relating in any way to AI.

## 7. Requests

To summarize, ACIA requests that you:

1. Strike the critical safety incident reporting requirements in Section 111, including the 15-day report to the CAISI Director and the 24-hour law enforcement clock.
2. Strike or make voluntary the frontier AI framework and transparency report mandates in Section 111.
3. Strike the independent verification organization licensing and audit regime in Section 112.
4. Strike Section 102, including the $100 million annual authorization, and decline to fund CAISI in appropriations.
5. Remove the three-year sunset on Section 121 and make preemption permanent, with a clarified development and deployment boundary.
6. Retain Titles III and IV, with Section 311 administered by CISA alone.
7. Narrow the definition of "AI violations" in Section 113.

GAAIA's best idea is one national standard. Its worst instincts are the mandates and the bureaucracy. Keep the first and strike the second, and this coalition will work hard to help you move the bill.

ACIA staff are available to walk through any provision, and to share the underlying survey data in aggregate form. Thank you for the chance to comment, and for the bipartisan seriousness this process reflects.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

cc: Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters

Contact: Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Comment letter: ACIA to Reps. Obernolte and Trahan

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
Washington, DC

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a discussion draft and for inviting stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington coalition of about 140 artificial intelligence developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture investors. Our members train the models, fabricate the chips and run the facilities behind American AI. Many are already living under the California and New York frontier laws that this draft would interact with, so our comments come from experience rather than theory.

Our position is straightforward. We support the preemption in Section 121 and most of Titles III and IV. We oppose the CAISI codification in Section 102 and the mandates in Sections 111 and 112, because they write an unfounded narrative about catastrophic AI risk into federal law. We ask you to strike those provisions, make preemption permanent, and keep the parts of the draft that actually help American builders.

## 1. The draft legislates a premise the evidence does not support

Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or of more than $1 billion in property damage. It defines "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of frontier model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. Section 101 also defines "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," language that reappears throughout Section 112.

Those definitions are the load-bearing wall of Title I. And they describe risks for which there is no evidence. No current or reasonably foreseeable AI system has caused a mass-casualty event or escaped human control. The scenarios that animate these provisions come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations. "Dangerous capability" evaluations and "scheming" studies are staged setups: they measure how a model behaves when researchers construct elaborate prompts inside fictional environments, which tells you little or nothing about how a deployed system behaves in the real world.

Congress should also ask who supplies these scenarios. The advocacy network behind them is small and unusually well funded. Open Philanthropy, renamed Coefficient Giving in late 2025, reported that its technical AI safety grantmaking rose from $46 million in 2024 to $157 million in 2025, across more than 200 grants. That money sustains a professional apparatus of grantees, coalitions and campaigns with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. Sections 102, 111 and 112 would convert that movement's premises into federal law, with a federal office, a licensed audit industry and a $100 million annual line item to enforce them.

Sections 111 and 112 sunset after three years. That is a telling admission: their authors expect the underlying evidence question to still be open in 2029. A mandate that cannot survive a reauthorization fight should not be enacted in the first place.

## 2. Our members are already paying for this narrative

ACIA surveyed its members in August 2026, and we are happy to share the aggregate results with your staff.

Among surveyed developers above $500 million in revenue that maintain a published frontier safety framework, the median estimated cost of keeping that framework current is $1.4 million per year. Across all surveyed developers, the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function is $310,000. Developers complying with the California and New York regimes in parallel report a median of 6.5 full-time employees devoted to that work. Thirty-four percent of surveyed startups say they delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and 61 percent of members cite conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem.

Those figures are the case for Section 121 and against Sections 111 and 112. A federal reporting mandate does not relieve the burden of state mandates. It adds a third layer on top of them, with federal penalties attached.

## 3. Preemption: support it, and make it permanent

We strongly support Section 121, which preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models while expressly preserving laws of general applicability, common law remedies, and state authority over AI use and deployment. California's SB 53 (Chapter 138 of 2025) has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour reporting clock. Developers cannot build against a map that redraws itself, and investors will not underwrite projects that face a new compliance cliff every few years.

Two changes would make Section 121 work as intended.

First, remove the three-year sunset. A preemption that expires in 2029 tells state legislatures to keep drafting, because their bills simply queue up for the day the freeze lifts. It also tells our members to keep paying for parallel state compliance, since the relief is temporary. The December 2025 executive order on a national policy framework for AI and the White House's March 20, 2026 legislative framework both argue that state laws imposing undue burdens should give way to a minimally burdensome national standard. GAAIA should deliver that, not a three-year truce.

Second, tighten the development and deployment line. An accompanying document from your offices acknowledges that California's AB 2013 training data disclosure law and a portion of SB 942 would be preempted. Statutory text should make clear that training, fine-tuning and pre-deployment evaluation are development activities, so companies are not litigating the boundary fifty times over.

## 4. Incident reporting: strike the Section 111 mandate

Section 111 requires every frontier developer, not only large ones, to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Combined with the civil penalty exposure elsewhere in the draft, reported at up to $1 million per day, this creates enormous liability attached to definitional disputes.

We ask you to strike it, for three reasons.

The definitions sweep in non-events. "Loss of control" and "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" are categories built for hypothetical scenarios, not documented ones. A company could be reporting, and paying penalties over, incidents that harmed no one.

Real incidents already have reporting channels. Unauthorized access to model weights is a computer intrusion, already a federal crime, and companies already report such intrusions to CISA and the FBI. A federal AI-specific mechanism adds a second, parallel obligation without adding a single responder.

And the mandate itself creates risk. A federal registry of AI security weaknesses, held by a new office with a small staff, is a target. Congress should not require companies to centralize sensitive security information with an agency that has no operational mission to use it.

## 5. CAISI: strike Section 102, and do not fund it

Section 102 codifies CAISI inside the Department of Commerce, hands it a portfolio of voluntary standards, system evaluation, monitoring of AI progress, synthetic content detection and the entire IVO licensing regime, and authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority charged to IVOs and large frontier developers. Your own FAQ notes that is an order of magnitude above the center's current roughly $15 million budget.

We ask you to strike the codification and the authorization, and we are asking appropriators not to fund the center at all. The administration created CAISI administratively in June 2025 out of the U.S. AI Safety Institute. There is no statutory gap to fill, and there is no evidence of harm that justifies a tenfold budget increase plus a permanent statutory home.

The White House's March 20, 2026 framework told Congress not to create any new federal rulemaking body to regulate AI. A licensed auditor regime supervised by a statutory CAISI is that body by another name. Section 112 would let the CAISI Director license independent verification organizations, send them into developers twice a year and on demand, and have them refer findings to the attorney general and state attorneys general. The auditors would depend on the office for their licenses and on the audited companies for their fees. That is textbook regulatory capture, and it would land on a handful of American developers while their foreign competitors face nothing comparable.

None of this means we oppose standards. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework worked precisely because it was voluntary, industry-led and usable. The International Organization for Standardization and the American National Standards Institute channels work, and the Title IV standards coordination that expressly excludes China is the right instinct. Keep that work voluntary and keep it at NIST's measurement science mission, not in a new federal AI safety bureau.

## 6. What we support and ask you to keep

We support Section 301, which extends the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035 so companies can share threat information without antitrust exposure. We support Section 311, authorizing CISA to grant funds to maintainers of widely used critical open-source software, though we would remove the CAISI consultation role. We support Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open-source security. We support the Title IV testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST and the National Science Foundation, the codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, and the international standards work that expressly excludes China. We support Section 122's Government Accountability Office review of federal AI adoption and of statutes that burden AI infrastructure, and Section 141's examination of agency pressure on AI platforms.

On Title II, we support better labor market data, including the Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics survey changes, and we would ask that it stay measurement rather than become a platform for new mandates. On Section 113, we support whistleblower protection and ask that "AI violations" be limited to violations of this Act rather than any violation of any federal law relating in any way to AI.

## 7. Requests

To summarize, ACIA requests that you:

1. Strike the critical safety incident reporting requirements in Section 111, including the 15-day report to the CAISI Director and the 24-hour law enforcement clock.
2. Strike or make voluntary the frontier AI framework and transparency report mandates in Section 111.
3. Strike the independent verification organization licensing and audit regime in Section 112.
4. Strike Section 102, including the $100 million annual authorization, and decline to fund CAISI in appropriations.
5. Remove the three-year sunset on Section 121 and make preemption permanent, with a clarified development and deployment boundary.
6. Retain Titles III and IV, with Section 311 administered by CISA alone.
7. Narrow the definition of "AI violations" in Section 113.

GAAIA's best idea is one national standard. Its worst instincts are the mandates and the bureaucracy. Keep the first and strike the second, and this coalition will work hard to help you move the bill.

ACIA staff are available to walk through any provision, and to share the underlying survey data in aggregate form. Thank you for the chance to comment, and for the bipartisan seriousness this process reflects.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

cc: Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters

Contact: Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Staff Q&A: GAAIA discussion draft

Prepared for ACIA staff ahead of Energy and Commerce meetings. Answers capped at 120 words.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.**

They answer different questions. Preemption is about jurisdiction: one national standard instead of fifty conflicting ones, and 61% of our members say conflicting state definitions are their top compliance problem. Incident reporting is a substantive mandate, and lighter is not the same as justified. Section 111 defines reportable events to include "loss of control" of a model and "failure of risk-mitigation measures," categories with no documented cases behind them, and it attaches penalties reported at up to $1 million per day. Federalizing a mandate does not fix its premise; it nationalizes it. Incidents that are real, such as stolen model weights, are already cyber intrusions that companies report to CISA and the FBI. Strike the provision.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?**

Obligations tied to harms we can point to. We accept federal enforcement of existing law against fraud, cyber intrusions and product defects, and GAAIA's Section 121 preserves state common law remedies and state authority over AI use and deployment, which is where actual consumer harms show up. We support voluntary, industry-led standards, which is how NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and the ANSI and ISO channels already work. We support Title III's open-source security grants and the testbeds in Title IV. What we cannot accept are mandates premised on "catastrophic risk" thresholds, pre-deployment gates, incident reporting to a new federal AI safety bureau, or a licensed auditor regime. Those all assume harms that have not occurred.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent: what is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?**

Permanent. A three-year sunset tells state legislatures to keep drafting, since their bills simply queue up for 2029, and it tells companies the relief is temporary so they should keep paying for parallel state compliance. Our members plan in cycles that dwarf three years: data center builds and chip programs run five to ten years, and no one sizes a capital project around a provision with an expiration date. The administration's own position, the December 2025 executive order and the March 2026 White House framework, treats state laws imposing undue burdens as a problem to be fixed, not paused. We would also like the development and deployment boundary clarified so the permanence is not litigated state by state.

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100 million per year. What is your view on the funding level?**

Zero. We asked the sponsors to strike Section 102 entirely, and we are asking appropriators not to fund the center. CAISI was created administratively in June 2025 out of the U.S. AI Safety Institute and runs on roughly $15 million today. A statutory home plus a tenfold authorization plus fee authority charged to audited companies is not a funding level, it is a new federal AI safety bureaucracy. The White House's March 2026 framework told Congress not to create a new federal rulemaking body for AI. If Congress wants to fund something at NIST, fund measurement science, and leave standard setting to voluntary, industry-led processes.

---
